title: Marketing Research Digest — Money & Spending — 2026-11-01
journals_not_indexed: Journal of Consumer Satisfaction, Dissatisfaction and Complaining Behavior
Journal of Empirical Generalisations in Marketing Science
Marketing Science Institute Working Paper Series

studies.title: "It's customary to leave a tip" beats appeals to reciprocity — and doesn't scare customers away
studies.paper_title: Injunctive Norms Outperform Reciprocity: Tip Request Messages Can Increase Tipping Without Reducing Demand
studies.the_study: Researchers ran what they describe as the first field experiments on tip request messages inside a global freelance marketplace, randomly varying three appeals: an injunctive norm ("It's customary to leave a tip for the seller's service"), personalized reciprocity, and impersonal reciprocity. The norms message produced the largest increase in tipping. Critically, it did so without depressing customers' returning demand on the platform.
studies.why_it_matters: Platforms have worried that nudging customers to tip will annoy them into buying less; this evidence suggests the right framing raises worker compensation without a demand penalty.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test the wording, not just the presence, of a tip prompt: norm-based language ("it's customary") outperformed reciprocity framing here, and the check-out prompt is one of the cheapest levers a platform has. Measure downstream repeat purchase, not just tip rate, before rolling it out.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Tipping prompts work on us largely because they signal what other people do — a reminder that "customary" is a powerful word, and worth noticing the next time a screen swivels toward you.
studies.caveats: Single platform (a global freelance marketplace) and a single service category; effects on tipping norms over longer horizons are not established.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, appeals and main result match the abstract; a mechanism claim and one caveat detail go beyond what the abstract states.

studies.title: Charging a penny for the second item beats giving it away free
studies.paper_title: Zero price or token price? The impact of bundle promotional format on promotional attractiveness and value discounting
studies.the_study: Across four experiments — two using imaginary purchase scenarios and two incentive-compatible — researchers compared "buy one, get one free" with token-price offers such as "buy one, get the second for only 1¢." Token-price promotions were consistently rated more attractive than freebies, whether the bonus item was identical to the focal item or different. But there was a long-run cost: when the two items were identical, token-price offers made consumers discount the value of the focal item more than freebies did; with nonidentical items the pattern reversed.
studies.why_it_matters: A penny is economically trivial but psychologically meaningful, and the same tweak that lifts short-term appeal can quietly erode what shoppers think the main product is worth.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you run BOGO mechanics, consider A/B testing a token price against free — but pair short-term redemption with a longer read on reference-price erosion, and note the finding that the bonus item being identical versus complementary flips the long-run effect.
studies.story_angle_secondary: "Free" isn't always the most tempting word in retail. Shoppers often respond more to a token price, even though paying a cent makes them objectively worse off — and it may reset what they believe the product is really worth.
studies.caveats: Two of the four studies used hypothetical scenarios; experiments are lab/online rather than real retail; country and category scope not specified in the abstract; no test of how the size of the token price changes the effect.
studies.verdict_notes: Four experiments, the attractiveness result and the reversal of value discounting are all reported correctly; one term is swapped ("complementary" for "nonidentical").

studies.title: Advice from friends pushes people into crypto; advice from professionals pulls them out
studies.paper_title: Personal advice vs. professional advice: how financial literacy moderates joint decision-making in cryptocurrency investment
studies.the_study: Using pooled cross-sectional data from 4,425 US respondents in the 2021 and 2024 National Financial Capability Study Investor Survey, researchers modeled how advice sources relate to cryptocurrency ownership. Personal advice from family and friends was positively associated with holding crypto; professional financial advice was negatively associated — a pattern robust across different household decision structures. Objectively measured financial and investment literacy weakened the pull of friends' advice, while people who merely believed themselves investment-savvy were less swayed by professional guidance.
studies.why_it_matters: It maps who actually moves retail investors into high-risk digital assets, and shows that self-assessed expertise — not real knowledge — is what makes clients tune out their advisers.
studies.story_angle_primary: For banks, brokerages and advisory brands: the competition for attention on speculative assets is peer networks, not rival firms, and clients with high subjective confidence are the hardest to reach. Worth testing communications designed for self-described experts, who discount professional advice most.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you got into crypto because a friend or relative told you to, you're in a statistically large group — and real financial knowledge, rather than feeling knowledgeable, is what helps people resist that social pull.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey data, so associations cannot establish causation (people may seek advice that matches decisions already made); US only; self-reported ownership and advice sources.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample, data source and both moderation results are accurately reported; headline and "Why it matters" use causal verbs the cross-sectional design cannot support, though Caveats do flag this.

studies.title: Malls are becoming schedules, not maps — and the order of activities changes what shoppers buy
studies.paper_title: Consumer scheduling of experiential activities in shopping centers
studies.the_study: Researchers extend store-choice theory to account for experiential, non-shopping activities in malls and city centers, arguing that such activities are discretionary, that time spent on them is a benefit rather than only a cost, and that consumers prefer particular, asymmetric orders of activities. An experiment in which participants scheduled a visit to their own city center supported the role of experiential activities in shaping which stores get visited, and follow-up simulations tested how store choices would shift if specific shopping or entertainment anchors were added.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives center managers a way to think about tenant mix and placement in terms of itineraries and sequencing rather than footfall alone — a cinema or restaurant doesn't just add traffic, it reorders the trip.
studies.story_angle_primary: Ask what your center's typical itinerary looks like, and where in the sequence your store sits: adding or relocating an entertainment anchor may redistribute store visits in ways a simple gravity model would miss. Simulation results are directional — worth validating against your own footfall and transaction data.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A trip to the mall or high street is increasingly planned like a day out, with coffee, a film or a meal slotted in a preferred order — and that order quietly determines which shops you end up walking into.
studies.caveats: Hypothetical scheduling exercise rather than observed behavior; single study area/city center; sample size and composition not reported in the abstract; store-choice shifts are simulated.
studies.verdict_notes: Theory summary and the scheduling experiment are described faithfully; the headline and consumer angle convert a theoretical proposition about activity order into a demonstrated effect on purchases.

studies.title: The cybersecurity paradox: for small, low-tech firms, protection spending can cancel out digital investment
studies.paper_title: Balancing risk and opportunity: Digital transformation, cybersecurity investments, and export performance in low-tech firms
studies.the_study: Analyzing Bank of Italy firm data from 2016 to 2023, researchers examined whether digital technology investment raises export sales in low-tech firms, and how cybersecurity spending conditions that return. Digital investment was positively associated with export sales where cybersecurity spending was absent, but the association turned negative in the highest protective-spending brackets, with the reversal located at the top of the distribution. The pattern was clearest among SMEs and manufacturers; among larger firms, digital investment showed no association with exports while protective spending was linked to higher export volume.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that for budget-constrained firms, security and digital growth compete for the same scarce money rather than reinforcing each other — a tradeoff rarely acknowledged in digital transformation pitches.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before signing off on parallel digital and cybersecurity programs in a resource-tight business unit, ask whether the two budgets are genuinely additive or drawing from the same pot; the data hint that heavy protective spending in small firms coincides with digital investment failing to translate into export growth.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Limited direct relevance for consumers, beyond context on why many smaller exporters struggle to turn technology spending into growth.
studies.caveats: Observational firm-level data from a single country (Italy) over 2016–2023; associations, not causal effects; data source is Bank of Italy survey data and firms self-report investment categories.
studies.verdict_notes: Findings, brackets and the SME/large-firm split are reported accurately and causal language is avoided; one caveat detail about the data is not in the abstract.

studies.title: When the app recommends you: what algorithmic visibility actually does for a local restaurant
studies.paper_title: Mobile Location-based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 16,720 restaurants around the official launch of a leading mobile location-based recommendation system, using the launch as quasi-experimental variation and a two-stage least squares instrumental-variable design to separate algorithmic exposure from underlying popularity. A 1% increase in exposure was associated with a 0.078% increase in clicks, and a 1% increase in clicks with a 0.053% increase in visit intentions. Exposure helped geographically disadvantaged restaurants most—but only at the discovery stage; conversion to an actual intended visit was stronger when a listing carried richer information and reputation signals such as reviews, owner-posted photos and menus. Credit-card sales data from a restricted Seoul subsample pointed to a positive link between exposure and real revenue.
studies.why_it_matters: It quantifies the split between being seen and being chosen: algorithms can hand a small business traffic, but the business still has to close the sale with content and social proof it controls.
studies.story_angle_primary: For brands and local operators dependent on platform discovery, the actionable implication is that paid or algorithmic visibility is only the first half of the funnel—audit the completeness of listing assets (photos, menus, review volume) before buying more exposure, and treat conversion-stage content as the variable you can actually control. Worth testing whether the same discovery-versus-conversion split shows up in your own category and platform.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The finding is a window into how recommendation apps reshape where people eat: being off the beaten path hurts less than it used to, but diners still hesitate to act on a nudge from an algorithm unless the listing gives them enough to go on—pictures, a menu, other people's reviews.
studies.caveats: Single platform and largely a single country (Korea, with the revenue evidence limited to a restricted Seoul credit-card subsample) and a single industry; the main outcome is clicks and stated visit intentions rather than confirmed visits; instrumental-variable estimates rest on modeling assumptions rather than a randomized design.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample size, elasticities, IV design and the discovery-versus-conversion split are accurate; one qualifier is tightened from "primarily" to "only".

studies.title: 1.7 million government contracts show who really wins when procurement is decentralized
studies.paper_title: Supplier Concentration in Decentralized Procurement: Evidence From a Low‐Institutional‐Capacity Context
studies.the_study: Using administrative records of more than 1.7 million public procurement transactions in Peru from 2015 to 2025, researchers tracked supplier concentration at the subnational level with several measures at once—Herfindahl–Hirschman Index, Gini coefficient, entropy and concentration ratios—looking at both contract value and contract frequency. Overall the market became less concentrated over the decade, but the pattern breaks down by contract size: for large contracts, the deconcentration trend vanishes once local market conditions are accounted for. The single strongest predictor of concentration was simply how many active suppliers a locality had, and big suppliers rarely survived a change of government term, hinting at political influence over high-value awards.
studies.why_it_matters: Public procurement is an enormous, often overlooked customer segment, and the data show that winning small contracts and winning large ones are governed by very different dynamics—market thinness for the former, political and institutional churn for the latter.
studies.story_angle_primary: For B2B and public-sector sales leaders, the takeaway to examine is that incumbency in large government contracts is unusually fragile across electoral cycles—pipeline models built on renewal assumptions may be mispriced, and the real growth opportunity may lie in thin local markets with few active suppliers.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Taxpayers get a concrete picture of how decentralized spending works in practice: more suppliers in a locality means more genuine competition, and the biggest contracts are the ones most likely to change hands when the government does.
studies.caveats: Single country (Peru) and a single procurement system; descriptive and correlational longitudinal analysis, so political influence over large contracts is inferred from turnover patterns rather than demonstrated causally; findings may not generalize to high-institutional-capacity settings.
studies.verdict_notes: Measures, period, concentration findings and the retention-rate inference all match; headline says "contracts" where the abstract says "transactions".

studies.title: The lifetime price tag of smoking, and what quitting at 25 versus 65 is worth
studies.paper_title: Potential cost saving associated with smoking prevention and cessation: an incidence-based cost-of-illness analysis in Thailand
studies.the_study: Health economists built a hybrid decision tree–Markov model to estimate the lifetime societal cost of smoking in Thailand, covering direct healthcare and indirect costs across four smoking-attributable diseases: COPD, lung cancer, ischemic heart disease and stroke. Lifetime excess costs came to roughly THB 0.93 million for men and THB 0.96 million for women (about US$26,000–27,000), with life expectancy cut by 9.54 years for men and 8.18 years for women. Savings from quitting fell sharply with age: men quitting at 25 saved about THB 0.58 million versus THB 0.04 million at 65; for women the figures were THB 0.67 million and THB 0.19 million.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a defensible per-person number on the economic value of early cessation, which is exactly the currency public health campaigns and finance ministries argue in when setting tobacco taxes and funding quit programs.
studies.story_angle_primary: For social marketers and health communicators, the steep age gradient suggests the persuasion budget belongs with the youngest smokers, where the economic return per convert is roughly ten to fifteen times higher—and gives campaign messaging a concrete monetary figure rather than an abstract health warning.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For individual readers the arithmetic is blunt: quitting in your twenties is worth more than half a million baht in avoided lifetime costs, and the financial case erodes decade by decade even though the health case never fully disappears.
studies.caveats: A simulation model, not observed behavior or spending; estimates depend on assumptions about disease incidence, costs and discounting; covers four diseases only, so total costs are likely understated; single country (Thailand) with cost structures that will not transfer directly elsewhere.
studies.verdict_notes: All cost, life-expectancy and cessation figures match the abstract, but the "ten to fifteen times" return multiplier holds only for men (for women it is roughly 3.5x).

studies.title: People are falling for AI companions — but they aren't letting them do the shopping
studies.paper_title: From AI boyfriends to AI shopping agents? The emerging convergence of relational AI and AI-assisted commerce
studies.the_study: Researchers tested whether "relational" AI (companion and romantic chatbots, including the "AI boyfriend" trend) is converging with agentic AI commerce, using three datasets: Google Trends search attention across six markets from 2020 to 2026; 44 AI-companion apps on Google Play; and 181,226 Reddit posts from relational-AI communities. Attention to both relational AI and AI commerce rose sharply and moved together, and the companion-app category showed heavy downloads and universal in-app purchasing — with romantic positioning carrying no adoption penalty. But no app marketed shopping as a core feature, and while about 9.1% of Reddit posts touched on commerce, only 0.3% showed the companion actually involved in a purchase decision.
studies.why_it_matters: Consumers are already paying real money inside emotionally intimate AI products, yet the obvious commercial next step — letting the companion recommend or buy things — remains almost entirely unbuilt, leaving an open and unclaimed channel.
studies.story_angle_primary: The paper names an "attention-market-integration gap": hype and revenue are running ahead of functionality. Brands should watch whether companion apps start bolting on commerce, and treat the 0.3% figure as a baseline to track rather than proof that users would welcome a partner-bot that sells to them — the trust backlash risk is untested.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For readers, it's a snapshot of a strange new spending category: millions of people are paying subscriptions and in-app fees to talk to an artificial partner, but they still draw a line at taking its shopping advice. The intimacy is monetized; the recommendations, so far, are not.
studies.caveats: Observational platform data, not an experiment — no causal claims. Confined to Google Play (no iOS), English-language Reddit communities, and six markets; Reddit users are not representative of companion-app users generally; Reddit commercial discourse was estimated through design-weighted coding rather than full manual review.
studies.verdict_notes: The three datasets and headline statistics are reported correctly, but the headline and consumer angle recast an absence of commerce functionality as consumers refusing it, and the Google Trends result is smoothed over.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- Other people's apparent behavior is the strongest spending lever in both digests. The norms message in "'It's customary to leave a tip' beats appeals to reciprocity" (W7224889302) and the peer-advice effect in "Advice from friends pushes people into crypto; advice from professionals pulls them out" (W7221884200) sit directly alongside the previous run's "Two different forces drive impulse buying in livestream auctions" (W7214649704), where envy of a winning bidder produced purchase urge on its own, and the social-norms component of "Young adults will take a mortgage but won't borrow from mum" (W7214655781).
- Felt expertise beats real expertise as a behavioral driver. The crypto advice study (W7221884200) finds that objectively measured literacy weakened the pull of friends while *subjective* investment confidence weakened the pull of professionals — the same comfort-versus-accuracy split flagged in "When AI gives you financial advice, explaining yourself works on feelings, not logic" (W7204478707) and consistent with the previous digest's finding that debt literacy reduced, rather than increased, receptivity to buffering credit (W7214655781).

**Advances**
- Experiential retail gets a mechanism at the trip level. "Malls are becoming schedules, not maps" (W7221500893) advances the thread opened by "When Tech in Stores Pays Off" (W7215084470) and "A pop-up store on tour cut the band's own online merch sales" (noted in prior continuity): where those showed physical and immersive experience is not reliably additive, the new work argues the determinant is sequence and itinerary — an entertainment anchor reorders the visit rather than simply adding footfall.
- Discovery versus conversion is now quantified. "When the app recommends you" (W7223381933) extends the pre-loaded-demand thread from "Those 'impulse' Shein hauls are actually carefully planned" (W7213342854) and the saved-ad finding in the prior run: exposure moves clicks, but conversion depends on assets the business controls — photos, menus, review volume. The earlier studies said discovery wasn't the bottleneck; this one separates the two stages statistically.

**Counterpoints**
- Parasocial attachment does not automatically become purchasing power. The previous digest showed attachment to a livestream host converting into impulse buying (W7214649704); "People are falling for AI companions — but they aren't letting them do the shopping" (W7223447670) finds deep emotional engagement and universal in-app spending with commerce influence at just 0.3% of relevant Reddit posts. Intimacy with a machine is monetizable as a subscription but, so far, not as a recommendation channel.
- "Free" loses to a penny. "Charging a penny for the second item beats giving it away free" (W7223666241) cuts against the affect-and-reassurance story that dominated the last run: here a purely numerical framing tweak outperforms, and the cost shows up later as reference-price erosion rather than in how the offer feels.

**New themes**
- Institutional and public money enters a topic that had been almost entirely consumer-facing: "1.7 million government contracts show who really wins when procurement is decentralized" (W7222602776) and "The cybersecurity paradox" (W7220422914) treat spending as a budget-allocation and market-structure problem rather than a psychology one.
- Health economics as spending evidence: "The lifetime price tag of smoking" (W7223008621) is the first per-person lifetime-cost modeling in this topic, with no counterpart in the previous digest.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Across this batch, machines and professionals are good at putting options in front of people and bad at closing them; other people close them. Algorithmic exposure lifted clicks for restaurants but converted only where human signals — reviews, owner photos, menus — were present ("When the app recommends you," W7223381933); friends moved people into crypto while professional advisers moved them out ("Advice from friends pushes people into crypto," W7221884200); a tip prompt worked best when it cited what other customers customarily do ("'It's customary to leave a tip,'" W7224889302); and users paying real money for AI companions almost never let them touch a purchase decision ("People are falling for AI companions," W7223447670).

**Why pitch this now:** Platforms and retailers are spending heavily on agentic AI commerce and recommendation surfaces on the assumption that an assistant people like will become an assistant people buy through — and this evidence says the trust needed for discovery is not the trust needed for conversion.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the trust hierarchy of spending — peers at the top, algorithms useful only as a shop window, professionals distrusted most by the people who think they know best, and AI companions monetized for intimacy but shut out of the cart. Written for platform, retail and financial-services strategists, with a consumer cut on why your friend's advice outranks your adviser's.

**Potential headlines:**
- Algorithms can get a business discovered, but reviews and photos still close the sale
- People will pay to date a chatbot and still won't let it pick dinner
- Your next expensive money mistake will probably be recommended by someone you know

**Potential outlets:**
- **Digiday** — tracking agentic commerce build-out closely; the discovery-versus-conversion split and the unbuilt companion-commerce channel are a direct challenge to the current pitch deck.
- **Marketing Brew** — strong on platform discovery mechanics for brands and local operators; the listing-assets-before-more-exposure finding is immediately usable for its readership.
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — the trust-hierarchy framing, including advisers losing self-described experts, is the kind of strategy-level synthesis it runs rather than a single-study item.
- **Wired** — covers AI companionship and the economics around it; the gap between monetized intimacy and zero purchase influence is a reported tech-culture story with hard numbers behind it.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **"It's customary to leave a tip" beats appeals to reciprocity (Work ID W7224889302):** First field evidence that norm wording, not reciprocity appeals, raises tips — and doesn't suppress repeat demand, killing the main objection platforms raise, for a marketing-trade news brief or a gig-economy/labor piece in a general-interest outlet.
- **Charging a penny for the second item beats giving it away free (Work ID W7223666241):** "Free" is not retail's most powerful word, and the token-price version quietly devalues the main product when the bonus item is identical, for a retail trade explainer or a consumer-psychology column on pricing tricks.
- **Advice from friends pushes people into crypto; advice from professionals pulls them out (Work ID W7221884200):** Self-assessed expertise — not actual knowledge — is what makes investors tune out advisers, a sharp hook for wealth-management and advisory audiences, for a banking/fintech trade column or a personal-finance feature.
- **Malls are becoming schedules, not maps (Work ID W7221500893):** Tenant mix as an itinerary problem rather than a footfall problem — where your store sits in the sequence of a day out, for a retail-property or retail trade explainer (flag that store shifts are simulated).
- **The cybersecurity paradox (Work ID W7220422914):** For small exporters, security and digitalization appear to compete for the same money instead of reinforcing each other, a counterweight to digital-transformation sales pitches, for an SME business or technology-strategy outlet.
- **When the app recommends you (Work ID W7223381933):** Quantifies what algorithmic exposure buys a local business — and shows off-the-beaten-path operators gain at discovery but still need reviews and photos to convert, for a local-commerce or platform-economy trade piece.
- **1.7 million government contracts show who really wins when procurement is decentralized (Work ID W7222602776):** Incumbency on big public contracts rarely survives a change of government, which makes renewal-based B2B pipeline forecasts look optimistic, for a public-sector/B2B sales column or a governance-and-transparency outlet.
- **The lifetime price tag of smoking (Work ID W7223008621):** A per-person monetary figure for quitting — roughly ten to fifteen times more valuable at 25 than at 65 — gives health communicators a number instead of a warning, for a public-health or social-marketing outlet, with a personal-finance cut.
- **People are falling for AI companions — but they aren't letting them do the shopping (Work ID W7223447670):** Millions paying subscriptions to an artificial partner, and essentially zero evidence they take its purchase advice — an unclaimed channel and an untested trust risk, for a tech-business brief or a consumer-technology explainer in a general-interest outlet.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Money & Spending — 2026-11-01
**Checked:** 2026-11-01 | **Studies reviewed:** 9
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: "It's customary to leave a tip" beats appeals to reciprocity — and doesn't scare customers away
**Work ID:** W7224889302 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Mechanism not tested in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Tipping prompts work on us largely because they signal what other people do"
- **Abstract says:** "Overall, the norms message increased tipping the most, and did so without reducing returning demand"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports which appeal performed best, not why; attributing the effect to social-signalling is an inference about mechanism that the abstract does not support.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "Norm-based wording outperformed reciprocity appeals here — a reminder that 'customary' is a powerful word" without asserting the psychological mechanism."

**Issue B. Unverifiable caveat detail** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Single platform (a global freelance marketplace) and a single service category"
- **Abstract says:** "field experiments ... in a global freelance marketplace"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not say the experiments were confined to one service category; a freelance marketplace typically spans many. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop "and a single service category" or mark it as not specified in the abstract."

### Study 2: Charging a penny for the second item beats giving it away free
**Work ID:** W7223666241 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Complementary" substituted for "nonidentical"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "note the finding that the bonus item being identical versus complementary flips the long-run effect"
- **Abstract says:** "when the two items are identical, consumers who encounter a token-price (vs freebie) promotion express stronger value discounting for the focal item. This effect reverses when the items are nonidentical. ... Future research should examine whether the bundle promotional format effect differs with ... the complementarity of the focal and supplemental items"
- **Problem:** The tested contrast was identical vs nonidentical items; complementarity is explicitly flagged as an open question for future research, so calling the second condition "complementary" misstates what was manipulated.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change "complementary" to "a different (nonidentical) item"."

**Issue B. Lab result generalized to shoppers** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Shoppers often respond more to a token price"
- **Abstract says:** "Two imaginary-scenario and two incentive-compatible experiments test the hypotheses."
- **Problem:** Findings come from scenario and lab-style experiments, not retail behavior; "shoppers often respond" implies a general field pattern.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "In these experiments, participants rated token-price offers as more attractive than freebies.""

### Study 3: Advice from friends pushes people into crypto; advice from professionals pulls them out
**Work ID:** W7221884200 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal phrasing for cross-sectional associations** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Advice from friends pushes people into crypto; advice from professionals pulls them out"
- **Abstract says:** "personal advice from family and friends is positively associated with cryptocurrency investment likelihood, whereas professional advice is negatively associated with it"
- **Problem:** Headline and "Why it matters" ("maps who actually moves retail investors", "is what makes clients tune out") assert causation from pooled cross-sectional survey data, contradicting the digest's own caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to "is linked to"/"goes with" in the headline and "Why it matters", keeping the body's associational wording."

### Study 4: Malls are becoming schedules, not maps — and the order of activities changes what shoppers buy
**Work ID:** W7221500893 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Order effect and purchase outcome overstated** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the order of activities changes what shoppers buy"
- **Abstract says:** "consumers may prefer to undertake experiential activities in particular, asymmetric orders. ... An experiment in which participants schedule a visit to their city center illustrates and supports the role of experiential activities in determining consumers' store choices."
- **Problem:** Asymmetric ordering is presented in the abstract as a theoretical proposition, and the empirical support concerns which stores are chosen in a hypothetical schedule — not what consumers buy.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe as "experiential activities shape which stores get included in a planned visit" and present the ordering claim as theory rather than a demonstrated purchase effect."

**Issue B. "Anchors" for "activities"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "follow-up simulations tested how store choices would shift if specific shopping or entertainment anchors were added"
- **Abstract says:** "Follow up simulations explore how store choices would change when specific shopping or entertainment activities are added to the study area."
- **Problem:** The abstract refers to adding activities to the study area, not anchor tenants; "anchors" implies a specific retail-property construct not tested.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "specific shopping or entertainment activities"."

### Study 5: The cybersecurity paradox: for small, low-tech firms, protection spending can cancel out digital investment
**Work ID:** W7220422914 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Data description not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "data source is Bank of Italy survey data and firms self-report investment categories"
- **Abstract says:** "Using Bank of Italy data (2016–2023)"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not describe the data as survey-based or self-reported. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "Bank of Italy firm-level data" without asserting survey design or self-reporting."

### Study 6: When the app recommends you: what algorithmic visibility actually does for a local restaurant
**Work ID:** W7223381933 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Only" overstates "primarily"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Exposure helped geographically disadvantaged restaurants most—but only at the discovery stage"
- **Abstract says:** "the estimated exposure effect is larger for geographically disadvantaged restaurants, but primarily at the discovery stage (clicks)"
- **Problem:** "Only" implies no benefit beyond clicks, whereas the abstract says the advantage was primarily — not exclusively — at discovery.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change "only at the discovery stage" to "mainly at the discovery stage"."

**Issue B. Country inferred** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "largely a single country (Korea, with the revenue evidence limited to a restricted Seoul credit-card subsample)"
- **Abstract says:** "Auxiliary credit-card sales data from a restricted Seoul subsample"
- **Problem:** The abstract names only the Seoul subsample; the country of the full 16,720-restaurant sample is not stated. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that only the Seoul subsample is identified by location in the abstract."

### Study 7: 1.7 million government contracts show who really wins when procurement is decentralized
**Work ID:** W7222602776 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Transactions labelled contracts** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "1.7 million government contracts"
- **Abstract says:** "administrative data from over 1.7 million transactions in SEACE"

### Study 8: The lifetime price tag of smoking, and what quitting at 25 versus 65 is worth
**Work ID:** W7223008621 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Multiplier wrong for women** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the steep age gradient suggests the persuasion budget belongs with the youngest smokers, where the economic return per convert is roughly ten to fifteen times higher"
- **Abstract says:** "for males, these ranged from THB 0.04 million (quitting at age 65 years) to THB 0.58 million (quitting at age 25 years). Among females, individuals who quit smoking at the same ages could save THB 0.19 million and THB 0.67 million, respectively."
- **Problem:** The 14.5x ratio applies to men only; for women the ratio of savings at 25 versus 65 is about 3.5x, so the stated range misrepresents the gradient for half the modelled population.
- **Suggested fix:** "State the gradient separately: roughly 14x for men and about 3.5x for women."

### Study 9: People are falling for AI companions — but they aren't letting them do the shopping
**Work ID:** W7223447670 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Absent functionality recast as user refusal** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "they still draw a line at taking its shopping advice"
- **Abstract says:** "no app positions shopping as a core feature ... design-weighted coding estimates 9.1% of corpus posts contain commercial discourse, but only 0.3% involve the companion itself in consumer or purchasing decisions"
- **Problem:** The low 0.3% figure reflects that shopping features are not built into these apps, not evidence that users reject them; the headline and consumer angle imply a consumer choice the data cannot show (the marketer angle notes this, so the two sections conflict).
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe as "companion apps haven't built shopping in yet" rather than "users won't let them shop"."

**Issue B. Google Trends result smoothed** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Attention to both relational AI and AI commerce rose sharply and moved together"
- **Abstract says:** "relational-AI attention rises significantly in five countries, AI-commerce attention rises in all six, with substantial but non-invariant temporal co-movement in attention"
- **Problem:** Drops that relational-AI attention rose significantly in only five of six markets and that co-movement was non-invariant across markets.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add "in five of six markets" and note that co-movement varied by market."

**Issue C. "Millions" of paying users** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "millions of people are paying subscriptions and in-app fees to talk to an artificial partner"
- **Abstract says:** "the category shows substantial downloads and spending ... in-app purchasing is universal"
- **Problem:** The abstract quantifies neither users nor payers; "millions ... paying" is an inference. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "the category shows substantial downloads and spending, with in-app purchasing available across every app examined"."
